Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
lowercase i need a prompt that gets a practical comparison of two wayfinding proposals for North Quay Bus Exchange, not a recommendation dressed up as a comparison. it is a municipal station in a coastal town, with twelve bus bays and an indoor concourse. Harbour Road is the east entrance and Market Lane is the west entrance. The ticket desk is just inside the east entrance. The toilets and the lift are near the middle of the concourse; stairs and another lift lead to the pedestrian bridge at the west end. At present the only route map is beside the ticket desk and the bay numbers are on signs overhead. There is a lot of engine noise when buses are pulling in, so spoken announcements can be hard to hear. Buses at bays 1 to 6 are frequent during the peak, usually every four to seven minutes, while bays 7 to 12 are used for less frequent coach services. On Saturdays the produce market crowds the pavement outside Market Lane, though that entrance stays open.

The two things to compare are proposals, not things already installed. Proposal A is a continuous teal floor stripe from both entrances, branching to each bay group and to the ticket desk, toilets and lifts. It also has overhead blade signs with bay numbers and destination names, a larger route map at each entrance, and smaller printed maps at the lift and ticket desk. The stripe would be interrupted where it crosses the boarding lanes, with matching arrows on the wall on either side of each interruption. The designer says people can follow a color route without needing to stop and read much, but that is a claim to assess against the details, not a proven result. The stripe is proposed as adhesive vinyl. The station manager says floor cleaning is done every night and that replacement vinyl is normally ordered in batches, rather than one small piece at a time.

Proposal B has no continuous floor line. It puts two large digital information kiosks in the concourse, one near each entrance, and freestanding printed maps at both entrances and beside the lift. It keeps the overhead bay-number signs but adds destination names beneath the numbers. A smaller screen would sit near the ticket desk. The kiosk design has a text search, a list of departures, and a route diagram; the designer says the screen can be updated when a bay changes. The proposal assumes staff can update it, but there is no supplied figure for staffing time or update costs. Printed maps would also be revised when the layout changes. The station manager says the concourse has power outlets by both entrances, but there is no information about network reliability or screen repair arrangements. Please don't fill those gaps with guesses.

Compare both proposals against the criteria I have supplied, not just which one sounds modern. The first criterion is route-finding: could a first-time passenger get from either entrance to the correct bay, ticket desk, toilets, or lift, including if they need to transfer between the frequent bays 1 to 6 and a coach at bays 7 to 12? Consider that overhead signs are already there and that the only current route map is by the ticket desk. The second is visibility and wayfinding under real conditions. Use the noise and Saturday market details where they matter, and consider that a passenger may arrive at either entrance. Don't assume every passenger will see or hear the same thing.

The third criterion is accessibility. Address mobility access, low vision, and passengers who may not read English well, but stick to what these proposals actually say. In particular, there is no specified tactile guidance, audio feature, set of languages, or screen-reader support. Don't award either proposal those features. The fourth criterion is disruption and installation: proposal A needs vinyl laid and signs or maps fitted, while proposal B needs kiosks and screens fitted. I don't have closure dates, contractor plans, or a disruption estimate for either, so mark those as unknown rather than estimating them. The fifth criterion is upkeep and operational fit: compare the stated nightly cleaning and batch ordering detail for vinyl with the stated map revisions, staff updates, power outlets, and missing network and repair information for the digital option. A sixth useful angle is whether the information stays consistent across signs, maps, and screens, but only discuss consistency based on the proposal details. Don't make up a workflow.

Please give a balanced comparison, with the criteria easy to find and the evidence for each option kept distinct from claims made by a designer. It would help to have a short opening that says what is being compared and a compact comparison table, followed by a numbered section called “Points to check before a decision.” Include the unanswered questions there, especially staffing time and costs for updates, network reliability, screen repairs, installation disruption, and any accessibility details not specified. I am not asking you to pick a winner or to invent a score. Keep the conclusion limited to what the supplied information supports, and clearly label unknowns. One staff member told me, “people follow the blue stripe until it stops at a boarding lane, then they look up,” but that was an observation, not a survey. A passenger at the ticket desk said, “I came in from Market Lane and didn’t know the map was all the way over here.” You can use those as reported remarks, not proof that everyone has the same experience. Please keep the comparison useful for a station team that has to discuss the two proposals, and don't add other proposals or extra criteria as if they had been provided.", "output": "Create a balanced, practical comparison of the two proposed wayfinding systems for North Quay Bus Exchange. Do not recommend a winner, assign scores, or treat design claims or individual remarks as proof. Use only the information below, distinguish stated facts from claims, and clearly identify missing information as unknown rather than guessing.

## Station context

North Quay Bus Exchange is a municipal station in a coastal town. It has twelve bus bays and an indoor concourse. Harbour Road is the east entrance; Market Lane is the west entrance. The ticket desk is just inside the east entrance. The toilets and one lift are near the middle of the concourse. Stairs and another lift lead to the pedestrian bridge at the west end. Currently, the only route map is beside the ticket desk, and bay numbers appear on overhead signs. Engine noise can make spoken announcements difficult to hear. During peak periods, buses at bays 1–6 usually arrive every four to seven minutes; bays 7–12 serve less frequent coach services. On Saturdays, the produce market crowds the pavement outside Market Lane, but that entrance remains open.

## Proposals to compare

**Proposal A:** A continuous teal floor stripe would run from both entrances and branch toward each bay group, the ticket desk, toilets, and lifts. Overhead blade signs would show bay numbers and destination names. Larger route maps would be placed at both entrances, with smaller printed maps by the lift and ticket desk. Where the stripe crosses boarding lanes, it would stop and matching arrows would appear on the wall on either side. The designer claims that people can follow a color route without stopping to read much; assess this claim against the supplied details rather than treating it as a proven result. The stripe would be adhesive vinyl. The station manager says floors are cleaned nightly and replacement vinyl is normally ordered in batches, not as individual small pieces.

**Proposal B:** There would be no continuous floor line. Two large digital information kiosks would be placed in the concourse, one near each entrance, with freestanding printed maps at both entrances and beside the lift. Existing overhead bay-number signs would remain, with destination names added beneath the numbers. A smaller screen would be placed near the ticket desk. The kiosks would have text search, departure lists, and a route diagram. The designer says the screen could be updated when a bay changes. The proposal assumes staff can update it, but no staffing-time or update-cost figures are supplied. Printed maps would also need revision when the layout changes. The station manager says power outlets are available by both entrances; network reliability and screen-repair arrangements are not specified.

## Comparison criteria

1. **Route-finding:** Consider whether a first-time passenger could get from either entrance to the correct bay, ticket desk, toilets, or lift, including when transferring between frequent services at bays 1–6 and a coach at bays 7–12. Account for the existing overhead signs and the current location of the only route map.
2. **Visibility and wayfinding in real conditions:** Consider the engine noise, the Saturday market crowd outside Market Lane, and the fact that passengers may enter from either side. Do not assume all passengers see or hear information in the same way.
3. **Accessibility:** Address mobility access, low vision, and passengers who may not read English well, using only the features actually specified. Neither proposal has specified tactile guidance, audio features, languages, or screen-reader support; do not attribute these features to either option.
4. **Installation and disruption:** Compare the stated work: laying vinyl and fitting signs or maps for Proposal A, and fitting kiosks and screens for Proposal B. Closure dates, contractor plans, and disruption estimates have not been supplied; identify these as unknown rather than estimating them.
5. **Upkeep and operational fit:** For Proposal A, consider nightly cleaning and batch ordering of replacement vinyl. For Proposal B, consider map revisions, staff updates, power outlets, and the missing information about network reliability and screen repairs.
6. **Information consistency:** Consider whether information would stay consistent across signs, maps, and screens, based only on the supplied proposal details. Do not invent an update workflow.

Start with a short statement of what is being compared. Then provide a compact comparison table, followed by a numbered section titled **“Points to check before a decision.”** Include unanswered questions there, particularly staffing time and update costs, network reliability, screen repairs, installation disruption, and unspecified accessibility details. Keep the conclusion limited to what the supplied information supports. Do not introduce other proposals or additional criteria.

Two remarks may be included as reported observations, not evidence of everyone’s experience. A staff member said, “people follow the blue stripe until it stops at a boarding lane, then they look up.” A passenger at the ticket desk said, “I came in from Market Lane and didn’t know the map was all the way over here.”"}]

That odd "lowercase" prefix is strange—it might just be a stray dictation artifact rather than a hidden instruction, so I shouldn't read too much into it. The rest of the input being fully capitalized is probably the more relevant detail to focus on.

Going through the pairs more carefully, I notice some details get dropped between input and output, like the specific cause of engine noise or the emphasis on not just favoring what sounds modern, but these omissions seem minor rather than substantive. Most other changes, like "could" versus "can," "would need revision," and distinguishing stated facts from claims, are faithful enough paraphrases that preserve the original meaning.

Still, dropping the station team audience context entirely feels like a real omission since it was a stated purpose for the comparison, not just stylistic flavor, and combined with the dropped noise condition, that's enough for me to call this pair a fail even though the output itself reads fine on its own, and the input had that lowercase anomaly making it uncertain.
